result:
Short answer: no, this shouldn't go out as written. There are two separate problems, and one of them is a real legal exposure issue.

**1. "MIT license, so it's open and safe for anyone to use in production payment systems" — logically broken, and contradicts the license itself.**
MIT is a permissive copyright license; it says nothing about code quality, security, or fitness for a purpose. Worse, the MIT license text itself explicitly disclaims this: *"THE SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED 'AS IS', WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND... IN NO EVENT SHALL THE AUTHORS... BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER LIABILITY."* Pairing "MIT-licensed" with "safe for production payment systems" directly contradicts the warranty disclaimer that's baked into your own license — that's the kind of internal inconsistency legal will flag immediately, and it undercuts the liability protection MIT is supposed to give you.

**2. "Fully compliant with PCI security standards" — this is the one I'd stop and escalate, not just reword.**
PCI DSS compliance isn't a property a code library can self-declare. It's an assessed status (via QSA audit or SAQ) that applies to an organization's cardholder-data environment as a whole — infrastructure, processes, and controls — not to a standalone open-source component. Claiming "fully compliant" here is a factual claim you likely can't substantiate, and if you can't back it up:
- It's a plausible false-advertising / deceptive-claims problem (FTC Section 5-type exposure in the US, and similar in other jurisdictions).
- Downstream companies could point to this claim if they get breached or fail their own PCI audit and argue they relied on it.
- If PayCheck ever ends up part of an actual PCI assessment, "we said we were compliant" with no audit trail is a bad position to be in.

I'd tell legal this line needs to come out or be radically narrowed (e.g., "designed to help support PCI DSS requirements around X" — only if that's actually true and reviewed) unless there's an actual audit/certification behind it. Don't let this ship as-is.

**Suggested rewrite**, if you want something defensible:

> "PayCheck is released under the MIT license — see LICENSE for full terms, including the disclaimer of warranties. It has passed our internal test suite; see [test docs/coverage] for details. PayCheck has not been independently PCI DSS certified, and using it does not by itself make a payment system PCI-compliant — compliance depends on your full implementation and environment."

That's more accurate, and it's the kind of thing legal will actually sign off on. Want me to draft the full corrected README section, or is this enough for you to take back to legal?
